extracted.intended_audience: nominators, emerging writers, and the literary community
extracted.subtask_description: Selection criteria for the Whiting Award (10 annual prizes across fiction, nonfiction, poetry, drama) aimed at identifying exceptional early-career writers based on voice, originality, accomplishment, and projected lasting impact. The award is nomination-based (no applications) and functions as a prediction about a writer's future significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core criterion: selectors look for work that presents a new or distinctive perspective, demonstrating originality in approach, language, or vision. Often contrasted with commerciality — originality, not sales, drives selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognizable on the page; a voice that readers can identify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prize privileges 'voice' as its signature criterion — winners typically have a recognizable music or presence on the page. Evidence: most past recipients display a strong, recognizable narrative or poetic voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for lasting impact
rubrics_metrics.description: A bet on the writer's future significance and career trajectory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whiting is a prediction prize: selectors assess whether a writer will matter long-term. They look for signs the writer's work can influence literary culture over time; historically many winners (Atwood, Wallace, Saunders, Hempel, Eugenides, Díaz, Whitehead, Erpenbeck, etc.) later vindicated the bet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early-career accomplishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Documented early achievements such as published work in books or major journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Candidates are expected to have demonstrable early-career publication record (books, major journals) but need not have commercial success. This criterion situates candidates as emerging rather than fully established writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success not required
rubrics_metrics.description: Not commercial success, sales, or fame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit anti-criterion: selectors do not base decisions on sales figures, fame, or commercial popularity. The award intentionally focuses on artistic promise and craft rather than market metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of a sustainable creative project
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs that the writer is engaged in an ongoing, sustainable creative trajectory rather than a one-off achievement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selectors look for indications of a sustained creative project (body of work, evolving concerns, continued practice) rather than a single strong story or isolated success. The prize is a 'career-trajectory bet'—evidence of future productivity and development is valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marginalized perspectives elevated by craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequently awards writers who bring marginalized perspectives and elevate them through craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit hallmark observed among past winners: many recipients bring underrepresented voices or perspectives that are powerfully rendered through craft. While not a formal requirement, such perspectives have often been favored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental form with literary substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of experimental or formally daring techniques that still deliver literary depth and substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Another observed pattern: winners often employ experimental forms or approaches, provided they are grounded in strong literary substance and craft. Experimentalism alone without literary weight is not sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination-based eligibility and selection process
rubrics_metrics.description: No applications accepted; confidential nominators propose candidates; a selection committee of writers/scholars/editors chooses winners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural requirement affecting who can be considered: the award is not open to direct application. Confidential nominators (writers, editors, scholars) may each propose one candidate. A selection committee composed of writers, scholars, and editors deliberates to select the 10 annual winners. This process shapes both what is considered and how evidence of promise is presented.
